segments.english: The LORD rained on Sodom and on Gomorrah brimstone and fire, from the LORD, from the heavens.
segments.literal: and-the-LORD rained on Sodom and-on Gomorrah brimstone and-fire from-with the-LORD from the-heavens

tokens.note: The vav is the conjunction; the divine name opens the clause as its subject.
qatal of the hifil of מָטַר, a verb from the noun for rain: the completed act, in narrative past.
Fire sent from heaven, the supernatural sense of the word.
מֵאֵת is 'from with': an idiom for 'from the side of'. Ibn Ezra reads it as 'from him'.

phrases.literal: 'and-the-LORD rained': the subject comes first, then the completed act
'on Sodom'
'and-on Gomorrah': the preposition repeated before the second city
'brimstone and-fire': the two things rained, without a preposition
'from-with the-LORD': the name is repeated as in the Hebrew; Ibn Ezra takes it as 'from him'
'from the-heavens': the place from which the fire came

grammar: The clause opens with the subject, and the qatal הִמְטִיר follows it. The qatal states the act as complete, and the narrative past is 'rained'.
The verb is hifil of מָטַר, a denominative of 'rain'. The hifil means to cause rain to fall, and עַל names the places on which it fell.
The etnaḥta on וָאֵשׁ marks the main division of the verse. The second half, מֵאֵת יְהוָה מִן הַשָּׁמָיִם, gives the origin twice, first with the idiom מֵאֵת and then with מִן.
The two origin phrases are parallel: מֵאֵת יְהוָה and מִן הַשָּׁמָיִם. The English keeps both, so the reader sees the same double statement.
segments.note: The English repeats 'the LORD' for מֵאֵת יְהוָה, as the Hebrew does. Ibn Ezra takes the repetition as elegant style (לשון צחות) for 'from him'; the English keeps the name so that the repetition he describes is visible. The decisions do not themselves require the name to be kept.

commentary.summary: Ibn Ezra: מֵאֵת ה' is an elegant turn of speech (לשון צחות); the sense is מֵאִתּוֹ, 'from him'. He adds that one finds 'the children of Israel' several times in a single verse. The English repeats 'the LORD', as the Hebrew does, and so follows him: it is the LORD who rains, and the repeated name is style, not a second person.

Rashi: it is the way of Scripture to speak so: 'wives of Lamech' and not 'my wives'; David says 'take with you the servants of your lord' and not 'my servants'; Ahasuerus has it written 'in the name of the king' and not 'in my name'. So here 'from the LORD' and not 'from me': God speaks of himself by name. The English keeps the third person.
Rashi: wherever 'and the LORD' occurs it means the LORD together with his court (בֵּית דִּינוֹ). The English takes the LORD himself as the subject, and the court reading is recorded here.
Rashi ties the time of the rain to the rising of dawn and gives a midrash on sun and moon. The English does not adopt it, and it does not bear on the plain sense.
Rashi: at first it was rain (בַּתְּחִלָּה מָטָר), and it became brimstone and fire. The English keeps the plain verb 'rained' and records his change of substance.
Rashi cites Job 36 and the manna of Exodus 16 on the way God sends punishment and gifts from heaven. This is a homily on God's ways and does not bear on the words.
Radak reads the one who acts as an angel called by the LORD's name, as he wrote at 18:3. The English keeps the LORD as the subject of the verb, and Radak's reading is recorded.

apparatus: 19:24.1 vowels: the WLC reads וַֽיהוָ֗ה; the base text reads וַֽיהֹוָ֗ה. The English is 'the LORD' in both.
context: The plain (הַכִּכָּר) is the district around the lower Jordan where the text places Sodom and Gomorrah (13:10–12). Chapter 14 names five cities of the plain, one of them Bela, which is Zoar (14:2, 8).
Brimstone (גָּפְרִית) is sulphur. Some readers take the fire and sulphur to be a natural catastrophe; the text names the LORD as the one who sent it, and the English follows the text.
In the text's picture of the world the heavens (שָׁמַיִם) are the sky above the earth, from which rain comes, and also the place where God is. Fire, like rain, comes down from there.

segments.english: He overturned these cities and all the plain and all the inhabitants of the cities and the growth of the ground.
segments.literal: and-he-overturned [ACC] the-cities these and-[ACC] all-of-the-plain and-[ACC] all-of dwellers-of the-cities and-growth-of the-ground

tokens.note: wayyiqtol of הָפַךְ, transitive: 'overturn, overthrow'. The subject is not named here; it is the LORD of v. 24.
הָאֵל is a rare short form of the demonstrative הָאֵלֶּה, 'these'; it follows its noun: 'the cities these'.
The vav and the object marker belong to the list of objects of the verb.
The vav and the object marker begin the second object of the list.
Participle of יָשַׁב, construct plural: 'the dwellers of'.
The construct noun צֶמַח, 'growth of', governs the next word.

phrases.literal: 'and-he-overturned': the wayyiqtol carries on the narrative from v. 24
[ACC]: the object marker, with no English counterpart
'the-cities these': the demonstrative follows its noun
'and-[ACC] all-of-the-plain': the second object, joined by the vav

phrases.english: and all the inhabitants of the cities
phrases.literal: 'and-[ACC] all-of dwellers-of the-cities': the third object, a construct chain

phrases.english: and the growth of the ground
phrases.literal: 'and-growth-of the-ground': the fourth object, a construct chain

grammar: The verse is a list of four objects of one verb. The first three are each marked by the object marker אֵת (the second and third joined by the vav as well); the fourth, וְצֶמַח הָאֲדָמָה, has the vav but no אֵת. The English keeps the repeated 'and all'.
The wayyiqtol וַיַּהֲפֹךְ continues the narrative from the qatal of v. 24 and gives the act: he overturned.
כׇּל־יֹשְׁבֵי הֶעָרִים is a construct chain: the participle יֹשְׁבֵי governs the noun 'the cities'. The English 'the inhabitants of the cities' keeps the chain.
The etnaḥta on הַכִּכָּר divides the verse. The tipḥa on צֶמַח, a construct, marks a pause before הָאֲדָמָה, and the silluq on הָאֲדָמָה ends the verse and the last object.

commentary.summary: Ibn Ezra: נשרפו האילנות, 'the trees were burned'. He takes וְצֶמַח הָאֲדָמָה as the trees of the ground, burned in the fire. The English 'the growth of the ground' is the general word, which covers the trees he names.
Rashi says the four cities sat on one rock and were overturned from top to bottom, and cites the verse of Job about the hand on the flint. This is an image, not the plain sense of the verb.

Radak: God turned the land from good to bad: it had been a land of pasture, 'all of it well watered' (13:10), and he rained brimstone and fire, burned it and felled all the cities and everything in them, men, beasts and the growth of the ground, so that the whole land was a burning and nothing grew in it again; its air too was burned, so that no bird flew over it (Job 28). That, he says, is the overthrow. The English keeps 'overturned' and records his wider reading.

context: The land of the plain had been well watered before the destruction (13:10). The text contrasts that earlier state with the ruin described here.

segments.english: His wife looked back from behind him, and she became a pillar of salt.
segments.literal: and-she-looked wife-of-him from-behind-him and-she-became pillar-of salt

tokens.note: wayyiqtol of the hifil of נָבַט, 'look'. The act is the one forbidden in v. 17, 'do not look behind you'.
The 3ms suffix refers to Lot, who is not named in the verse.
מֵאַחֲרָיו: 'from behind', with the 3ms suffix; 'him' is Lot.
wayyiqtol of הָיָה, 'become', followed by a predicate noun with no verb between.

phrases.english: His wife looked back from behind him
phrases.literal: 'and-she-looked wife-of-him from-behind-him': the verb first, then the subject, then the place

phrases.english: and she became a pillar of salt
phrases.literal: 'and-she-became pillar-of salt': the predicate noun completes the verb

grammar: The verse is two wayyiqtol clauses. The first gives the look, the second the change, and the English keeps the order.
The verb of the second clause is 'be' in the sense 'become', and the predicate נְצִיב מֶלַח is a noun phrase: pillar of salt.
The etnaḥta on מֵאַחֲרָיו divides the verse. The first half ends with the place of the look, and the second half gives the result.
The Hebrew says 'his wife', not Lot's wife, and the English keeps 'his wife'. The reader is told whose wife she is only by the suffix.

commentary.summary: Ibn Ezra: מֵאַחֲרָיו means 'from behind Lot'. The English 'from behind him' keeps the pronoun, and the reader takes it as Lot.

Ibn Ezra: נְצִיב is in the sense of מַצֵּבָה, a standing monument, because her substance was burned in the brimstone and she was with salt, for it is written 'brimstone and salt ... like the overthrow of Sodom' (Dt 29:22). He adds that this verse also shows she had escaped as far as Zoar, as the angel too said. The English 'pillar' keeps the sense of a standing monument.

Radak glosses נְצִיב מֶלַח as like תֵּל מֶלַח, a mound of salt; his next comment (19:26:3) adds that she stood upright when she looked back and so turned to salt in her stature. Radak thus gives the form as a mound but a standing one; the English 'pillar' keeps the standing form and records his 'mound'.
Rashi's midrash says she sinned with salt, refusing it to guests, and was punished with salt. This is a homily on her deed and does not bear on the plain sense.
Radak on נְצִיב: as she stood upright when she looked behind her, so she turned to salt in her stature (בקומתה). This is a standing figure, and the English 'pillar' follows it.

context: Brimstone and salt are named together in Deuteronomy 29:22 as the ruin of a land overthrown by God, so salt belongs to the picture of the destruction in the text.

The word נְצִיב is used elsewhere of an officer or garrison posted in a place; its root is נצב, 'stand'. Here it is a standing figure of salt. Ibn Ezra takes it as a monument (מַצֵּבָה), Radak compares a mound (תֵּל) of salt and says she became salt standing; the English has 'pillar'.
The shores of the Dead Sea have large deposits of salt, and many readers connect the story with such formations; the text itself does not say so.

segments.english: And Abraham rose early in the morning and went to the place where he had stood before the LORD.
segments.literal: and-rose-early Abraham in-the-morning to the-place which he-stood there before-face-of the-LORD

tokens.note: The hifil of שָׁכַם, 'rise early', used as an adverb of the action; the wayyiqtol carries on the narrative.
The standing-place: the place where Abraham had stood before the LORD (18:22).
The relative particle introduces a clause about the place.
qatal of עָמַד: 'had stood', a past perfect in English.
שָׁם, 'there', repeats the place named by הַמָּקוֹם; English does not need it and leaves it out.
אֵת פְּנֵי here marks the idiom of standing in the presence of someone.
The construct of פָּנֶה, 'face', in the sense 'presence'.

phrases.english: And Abraham rose early in the morning
phrases.literal: 'and-rose-early Abraham in-the-morning': the verb opens, then the subject and the time

phrases.english: and went to the place where he had stood
phrases.literal: 'to the-place which he-stood there': the Hebrew has no verb of motion after וַיַּשְׁכֵּם, only אֶל; the English supplies 'went'. The resumptive 'there' is not repeated
'before-face-of the-LORD': the idiom of standing in the presence of a superior

grammar: The verb וַיַּשְׁכֵּם is a hifil wayyiqtol. 'Rose early' is an idiom, with the time phrase 'in the morning' after it. No verb of motion follows; אֶל־הַמָּקוֹם carries it, and the English adds 'went'.
The relative clause אֲשֶׁר עָמַד שָׁם is a qatal with an adverb: 'where he had stood', with שָׁם repeating the place.
The phrase עָמַד אֶת־פְּנֵי יְהוָה, 'stood before the LORD', names the place as the one where Abraham stood in 18:22; there the wording is עֹמֵד לִפְנֵי יְהוָה, here אֶת־פְּנֵי.
The zaqef qaton on הַמָּקוֹם and the tipḥa on שָׁם divide the relative clause. The silluq ends the verse on the divine name.

commentary.summary: Radak cross-refers to 18:22, where Abraham still stood before the LORD, and says this is the place the angels parted from him. The cross-reference is accepted as the place, and it does not change the words.
Radak takes the early rising as the basis of the morning prayer, which the Sages ascribe to Abraham. This is a note on later practice and does not bear on the plain sense.

Sforno: 'to the place where he had accompanied the angels', for there the hand of the LORD had been upon him; he meant to ask mercy for the cities, having found no merit in them at judgment. The motive is not in the Hebrew, so the English does not state it.

context: To stand before a god or a king in the Hebrew Bible is the posture of an attendant or a petitioner. Here the place is the one where Abraham stood before the LORD to plead for the cities (18:22–33).

segments.english: And he looked down over the face of Sodom and Gomorrah, and over all the face of the land of the plain. And he saw, and look, the smoke of the land rose like the smoke of a furnace.
segments.literal: and-he-looked-down upon face-of Sodom and-Gomorrah and-upon all-face-of land-of the-plain and-he-saw and-look rose smoke-of the-land like-smoke-of the-furnace

tokens.note: wayyiqtol of the hifil of שָׁקַף, 'look down'.
The face, here the surface of the ground over the cities.
אֶרֶץ הַכִּכָּר: the district or region of the plain.
wayyiqtol of רָאָה, 'see'.
הִנֵּה introduces the thing seen: 'look'.
qatal after הִנֵּה: what Abraham saw, the smoke going up; English 'rose'.
The preposition כְּ introduces the simile.
כִּבְשָׁן, 'kiln', taken as a fire-place that burns constantly (Ibn Ezra).

phrases.english: And he looked down over the face
phrases.literal: 'and-he-looked-down upon face-of': the verb, then the preposition and the noun
'Sodom and-Gomorrah'

phrases.english: and over all the face of the land of the plain
phrases.literal: 'and-upon all-face-of land-of the-plain': the second clause of the same look
'and-he-saw and-look': the seeing and what is seen

phrases.english: the smoke of the land rose
phrases.literal: 'rose smoke-of the-land': the verb first, then the subject

phrases.english: like the smoke of a furnace
phrases.literal: 'like-smoke-of the-furnace': the simile

grammar: The two wayyiqtol verbs, וַיַּשְׁקֵף and וַיַּרְא, give the look and the seeing in sequence.
The repeated noun פְּנֵי ('face') means the surface of the ground over the cities. The English repeats 'over the face of' to keep the parallel.
וְהִנֵּה introduces the seen thing. Its qatal עָלָה is rendered 'rose': after הִנֵּה the qatal states what is there to be seen.
The etnaḥta on הַכִּכָּר ends the first half of the verse, the looking; the second half gives what he saw. The silluq closes the verse on הַכִּבְשָׁן.

commentary.summary: Ibn Ezra: כְּקִיטֹר means 'like smoke', of the same root as incense (קְטֹרֶת). The English keeps 'smoke'.
Ibn Ezra: הַכִּבְשָׁן is a place where fire burns always. The English takes it as 'the furnace', a fire-place kept burning, and Rashi's lime-kiln reading is recorded below.
Rashi glosses קִיטוֹר as תִּמּוּר של עָשָׁן, a column of smoke. The English says 'smoke' and does not take the column.
Rashi: הַכִּבְשָׁן is a pit in which stones are burned to make lime, and so every kiln in the Torah. The English takes 'furnace' on Ibn Ezra's reading, and Rashi's lime-kiln is the alternative.
Radak: קִיטֹר הָאָרֶץ is the smoke from the burning that burned the land. The English 'the smoke of the land' keeps the same sense.
Sforno reads the look as a gaze of enmity (הַשְׁקָפַת אֵיבָה) at their great wickedness. The English gives the plain verb 'looked down' and records his reading.

Radak: a כִּבְשָׁן is where stones are burned to lime, or where pots are fired. The English 'furnace' follows Ibn Ezra's general 'place of fire'; Radak's lime-kiln or potter's kiln is the alternative.

context: A kiln (כִּבְשָׁן) was used to burn stone to lime or to fire clay. Exodus 19:18 uses the same word for the smoke of Sinai, so the simile is a sight the first readers knew.
The word translated 'furnace' in the English is the word for a kiln. Its use for a fire kept burning, as Ibn Ezra takes it, is a reading, not a fact of the text.

segments.english: When God destroyed the cities of the plain, God remembered Abraham and sent Lot out of the midst of the overthrow, when he overturned the cities in which Lot had lived.
segments.literal: and-it-came-to-pass in-destroying God [ACC] cities-of the-plain and-he-remembered God [ACC] Abraham and-sent [ACC] Lot out-of-midst-of the-overthrow in-overturning [ACC] the-cities which dwelt in-them Lot

tokens.note: wayyiqtol of הָיָה with בְּ and an infinitive: 'when'. The idiom becomes the English temporal clause.
בְּ with the piel infinitive construct of שָׁחַת: 'in ruining'. The clause is temporal.
אֱלֹהִים, the God of Israel: 'God' (decisions).
wayyiqtol of זָכַר with God as subject, 'remember'.
wayyiqtol piel of שָׁלַח, 'send out'.
מִתּוֹךְ: 'from the midst of'.
הֲפֵכָה, from the root of the verb in v. 25.
בְּ with the qal infinitive construct of הָפַךְ: 'in overturning'. The clause is temporal.
The relative particle. Ibn Ezra reads the clause as 'in one of which', below.
qatal of יָשַׁב, 'dwell'.
בָּ with the 3fp suffix; 'them' are the cities.

phrases.english: When God destroyed the cities of the plain
phrases.literal: 'and-it-came-to-pass in-destroying God [ACC] cities-of the-plain': a temporal clause, with the verb in the infinitive
'and-he-remembered God [ACC] Abraham': the main clause
'and-sent [ACC] Lot': the second verb of the main clause

phrases.english: out of the midst of the overthrow
phrases.literal: 'out-of-midst-of the-overthrow': where Lot was taken out from
'in-overturning [ACC] the-cities': the second temporal clause
'which dwelt in-them Lot': the relative clause; the plural בָּהֵן is kept. Ibn Ezra reads it as 'in one of them' (Lot lived in Sodom only); that is his explanation, recorded in the commentary.

grammar: The sentence has two temporal clauses, both built with בְּ and an infinitive construct: 'when God destroyed' and 'when he overturned'. The English makes both 'when' clauses.
The main clause has two verbs, וַיִּזְכֹּר and וַיְשַׁלַּח: God remembered Abraham and sent Lot out. The cause and the result are joined by the vav.
The noun הֲפֵכָה and the infinitive בַּהֲפֹךְ share the root of the verb in v. 25, so the 'overthrow' is the same act as the overturning.
The etnaḥta on אַבְרָהָם divides the verse: the first half is the remembering, and the second half is the sending and the overturning.

commentary.summary: Ibn Ezra reads אֲשֶׁר בָּהֵן as 'in one of them' (באחת מהן): Lot lived in one of the cities. He cites Judges 12:7, Zechariah 9:9 and Leviticus 20:14 for a plural standing for a singular. The English keeps the plural of the Hebrew, 'in which Lot had lived'.
Radak glosses מִתּוֹךְ הַהֲפֵכָה as 'before the overthrow came'. The English keeps 'out of the midst of the overthrow', the literal sense, and records Radak's reading.

Radak glosses בַּהֲפֹךְ אֶת־הֶעָרִים as 'at the time when he wished to overturn', not 'while he overturned', since the angel said 'I cannot do anything until you come there' (19:22): Lot was brought out before the overturning began. The English 'when he overturned' keeps the plain tense and records his reading.

context: In this text God 'remembering' someone is God acting on a commitment to that person; it is not a recalling of something forgotten (compare Noah, 8:1).

segments.english: And Lot went up from Zoar and dwelt in the mountain, and his two daughters with him, because he feared to dwell in Zoar, and he dwelt in the cave, he and his two daughters.
segments.literal: and-went-up Lot from-Zoar and-dwelt in-the-mountain and-two daughters-of-him with-him for feared to-dwell in-Zoar and-dwelt in-the-cave he and-two daughters-of-him

tokens.note: wayyiqtol of עָלָה, 'go up', of leaving the town for the hill.
מִ + צֹעַר. The text names Zoar as a small town (19:20, 'is it not small').
wayyiqtol of יָשַׁב, 'dwell'.
הָהָר, the mountain the angel named (19:17).
כִּי with a qatal: the causal clause that follows.
qatal of יָרֵא, 'fear, be afraid'.
לְ with the qal infinitive construct of יָשַׁב.
wayyiqtol of יָשַׁב, 'dwell', now in the cave.
The independent pronoun הוּא follows the verb and resumes the subject, so that the daughters can be added to it: 'he and his two daughters'.

phrases.english: And Lot went up from Zoar
phrases.literal: 'and-went-up Lot from-Zoar'
'and-dwelt in-the-mountain'

phrases.english: and his two daughters with him
phrases.literal: 'and-two daughters-of-him with-him': the subject of the accompaniment

phrases.english: because he feared to dwell in Zoar
phrases.literal: 'for feared to-dwell in-Zoar': the causal clause

phrases.english: and he dwelt in the cave
phrases.literal: 'and-dwelt in-the-cave'
'he and-two daughters-of-him': the independent pronoun, then the daughters

grammar: Three wayyiqtols move the narrative: Lot went up, he dwelt in the mountain, and he dwelt in the cave.
The clause כִּי יָרֵא לָשֶׁבֶת gives the reason: 'for he feared to dwell'. The infinitive construct with לְ is the object of the fear.
The independent pronoun הוּא comes after the verb and resumes the subject, so the English 'he and his two daughters' repeats the subject.
The etnaḥta on בְּצוֹעַר divides the verse, and the silluq on בְנֹתָיו ends it with the daughters.

commentary.summary: Rashi: Lot feared to dwell in Zoar because it was near Sodom. The English states the fear without a reason, and Ramban's different reason is recorded.

Ramban rejects Rashi's reason: Zoar was among the places marked for overthrow, and it was spared only at Lot's plea. Lot feared that the delay would not last, since he had time to reach the mountain. The English does not choose between them.
Radak identifies the mountain as the one the angel had named (19:17). This cross-reference does not bear on the English words.

context: Zoar is named in the text as a small town that Lot asked to be spared (19:20–22); the text ties its name to the word 'small' (19:20, 22). It is the Bela of 14:2, 8.
Caves in hill country served as shelter and dwelling places.

segments.english: And the firstborn said to the younger, "Our father is old, and there is no man in the land to come to us as is the way of all the earth.
segments.literal: and-she-said the-firstborn to the-younger our-father old and-man there-is-not in-the-land to-come upon-us as-way-of all-the-earth

tokens.note: wayyiqtol of אָמַר, 'say'.
הַבְּכִירָה, feminine: the elder daughter.
הַצְּעִירָה, feminine: the younger daughter.
qatal of זָקֵן used as a stative: 'is old'.
אֵין, the negative existential: 'there is no'.
לְ with the qal infinitive construct of בּוֹא, 'come'. With עַל it is a euphemism for sexual relations.
עָלֵינוּ: 'upon us', with the verb of motion, 'come to us'.
כְּ with דֶּרֶךְ: 'in the way of', 'as is the custom of'.

phrases.literal: 'and-she-said the-firstborn': the verb first, then the speaker; הַבְּכִירָה is the elder of the two
'to the-younger'
'our-father old': the speech begins

phrases.english: and there is no man in the land
phrases.literal: 'and-man there-is-not in-the-land': the existential clause
'to-come upon-us': a euphemism for sexual union

phrases.english: as is the way of all the earth
phrases.literal: 'as-way-of all-the-earth': the custom the speaker takes for granted

grammar: The speech is the words of the elder daughter, in direct speech after the verb of saying. The English gives them in double quotation marks.
אָבִינוּ זָקֵן: the qatal of זָקֵן is stative, 'is old', and the subject 'our father' is first. The speech is a reason for what follows.
לָבוֹא עָלֵינוּ: 'come upon us' is an idiom; in this context it is a euphemism for sexual union, here with the aim of children. The English 'come to us' keeps the euphemism.
כְּדֶרֶךְ כׇּל־הָאָרֶץ: 'as is the way of all the earth'. The custom is taken for granted and the text does not describe it. The plan that follows is in v. 32.

commentary.summary: Ibn Ezra: the daughters thought fire and brimstone had covered all the land, like the flood of waters, so that no one was left. He also suggests, as a possibility, that Lot had another wife who died first. The English adopts the first reading, and the earlier wife is not adopted; Ramban rejects it, since 'firstborn' is only the elder.
Rashi: the daughters thought the whole world had been destroyed, as in the generation of the Flood (Genesis Rabbah). The English keeps the daughters' words without the midrash.

Radak: most commentators say the daughters thought the whole land was like Sodom and Gomorrah, with no man or woman left; he calls this far-fetched, since they had come out of Zoar, which was not overturned, and they had heard from their father that the cities were overturned for their people's wickedness. He prefers what he heard in the name of Joseph Kara: the elder meant that no man would want to take them as wives, since people would say they were of the men of the overturning. The English keeps the words general and records the reading.
Rashi glosses the daughters' reason: 'if not now, when?', lest their father die or stop begetting. This gives their motive, which the English does not state.

context: The daughters speak of 'coming in to' a woman as the normal way to marriage and children. In the text's world a family was continued through its children, and marriages were arranged by the father; the text gives their words without comment.
